facts.text: Reference for drafting legal-adjacent prose that will go to counsel: contracts, disclaimers, privacy notices, breach disclosures, and regulator-facing statements. This skill is craft for drafts, not legal advice. Every output should carry a "counsel must review before execution" footer.
Is the risk-allocating verb correct? "Shall," "will," "must," and "may" are not synonyms. Modern drafting prefers "must" over "shall" because "shall" has been litigated into ambiguity.
Are the defined terms actually defined? Every Capitalized Term should appear once in a Definitions section.
Does the carve-out language survive a hostile read? "Except for" should be paired with a non-exhaustive list ("including but not limited to") only when you want breadth.
Is the temporal scope explicit? "In the 12 months preceding the event giving rise to the claim" is unambiguous. "In the prior year" is ambiguous.
Is the notice-and-cure mechanism workable? If a clause requires "written notice," specify the delivery channel, the recipient, and the cure window.
Cap amount. Most common SaaS form: "fees paid by Customer in the 12 months preceding the event."
Damages exclusion. "No indirect, incidental, special, consequential, or punitive damages, including lost profits."
Carve-outs. Standard market carve-outs: breach of confidentiality, breach of IP indemnification, payment obligations, gross negligence, willful misconduct, death or personal injury.
The standard pattern:
The all-caps formatting is not stylistic. It is a UCC § 2-316 "conspicuousness" requirement.
The SEC's 2023 cybersecurity rules require public companies to file a Form 8-K within four business days of determining that a cybersecurity incident is material.
What must be disclosed:
The material aspects of the nature, scope, and timing of the incident
The material impact or reasonably likely material impact on the registrant
What is NOT required: specific technical detail about the attack vector, specific detail about cybersecurity systems, or any detail that would impede ongoing remediation.
GDPR Article 33 requires controllers to notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach "without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it."
Phased notification is explicitly permitted. Article 33(4) allows you to provide information "in phases without undue further delay."
The notification must include:
Name and contact details of the DPO
Likely consequences of the breach
Measures taken or proposed
Required components under GDPR Article 13/14:
Identity and contact details of the controller
Purposes of processing and legal basis for each
Recipients or categories of recipients
Storage period or criteria
Right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority
Mixing "shall" and "must" within the same document. Pick one register.
The "reasonable" undefined. "Commercially reasonable" should be defined or paired with a benchmark.
Non-conspicuous warranty disclaimers. A disclaimer that is not in all caps may be ignored under UCC § 2-316.
Promising what you can't deliver in a privacy notice. "We will never share your data with anyone" creates a contractual representation.
Stuffing technical detail into an 8-K cyber disclosure. Describe impact, not mechanism.
> This is draft language only. It is not legal advice. Qualified counsel must review before execution, filing, or public release.

UCC § 2-316 (conspicuous disclaimer of implied warranties)
Drafting a SaaS limitation-of-liability clause or warranty disclaimer that needs to survive both a hostile legal read and a UCC conspicuousness requirement before it goes to counsel.
